title: Echolocation: how bats and dolphins see with sound
description: Bats and dolphins navigate in darkness by shouting at the world and listening to the echoes that bounce back.

body.heading: Shouting to see
paragraphs: Echolocation is a way of sensing the world with sound. The animal makes a short, sharp click and listens to the echo. The time the echo takes to return tells it how far away the object is; differences between its two ears give direction; the echo's tone reveals size and texture.

Most bats call in ultrasound, at frequencies far above human hearing — which is why a summer evening can be full of hunting bats in apparent silence. As a bat closes on a moth, its calls speed up into a rapid buzz, updating the picture many times a second. In the final moment before contact, that buzz can reach hundreds of calls per second.

body.heading: Dolphins and the melon
paragraphs: Toothed whales and dolphins echolocate underwater, where sound travels well but light fades fast. A dolphin makes clicks in its nasal passages and focuses them into a beam using the melon, a fatty dome on its forehead that works like a lens for sound.

The returning echoes are picked up through the jaw and give a remarkably detailed picture: dolphins can find a small fish buried in sand, and can tell apart objects that differ only in the material they are made from.

body.heading: Countermeasures in the dark
paragraphs: The system is so effective that prey have evolved defences. Many moths have ears tuned exactly to bat frequencies, and dive or loop when they hear a call. Some tiger moths answer with clicks of their own that jam the bat's sonar, scrambling its picture.
Humans borrowed the idea: sonar on ships and ultrasound scans in hospitals both work by sending out sound and reading the echoes — echolocation, rebuilt in electronics.

takeaway: Echolocating animals emit clicks and read the returning echoes to judge distance, direction and texture, building a sound-picture of their surroundings.
